summary: Describes an architecture for creating and maintaining Service Function Chains, in which traffic passes through an ordered set of services. It covers concepts, principles and components, and does not propose protocols or solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: Service Function Chaining arranges network services, such as firewalls, in a chosen order and steers selected traffic through them. RFC 7665 defines the concepts and components for this architecture, including classifiers, forwarders, and an encapsulation that identifies the path. It does not specify a protocol or a complete solution.

subtitle: An architecture for steering traffic through an ordered set of network services.

tldr.problem: Traditional service functions are often tied to fixed network locations, making it difficult to change or dynamically compose services.
tldr.mechanism: A classifier assigns traffic to a Service Function Path, and Service Function Forwarders use an SFC encapsulation to steer packets through selected service functions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7665 defines concepts, principles, and components, but proposes no protocols or solutions. Its scope is a single network administrative domain.

facts.label: SFC encapsulation role
facts.value: Identifies the SFP; not used for packet forwarding

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
A network service may require several service functions, such as a firewall or network address translator. Service Function Chaining (SFC) defines an ordered set of these functions and steers selected traffic through them.

The architecture separates service paths from the underlying forwarding topology. It applies to fixed and mobile networks and data centers, but assumes one administrative domain; inter-domain SFC is left for future study. RFC 7665 describes concepts and components, not protocols or solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: SFC gives an operator a way to select services for traffic and choose their order. The architecture is designed to avoid tying that service order to the network's physical layout.

sections.title: Chains, Paths, and Rendered Paths
sections.content:
A Service Function Chain (SFC) is an abstract ordered set of service functions and ordering constraints. A chain may branch, and a function may appear more than once. Chains may be unidirectional, bidirectional, or hybrid.

A Service Function Path (SFP) applies policy to a chain and may specify exact functions and forwarders or leave some choices open. A Rendered Service Path (RSP) is the actual sequence of service functions and forwarders a packet visits. These terms describe successive levels of detail.
sections.plainLanguage: A chain says which functions traffic needs and in what order. A path adds deployment choices, and a rendered path records the exact functions and forwarders a packet visits.

sections.title: Components and Packet Handling
sections.content:
A classifier matches traffic to policy and assigns it to an SFP. The SFC encapsulation identifies that path and can carry metadata, but it is not used by the network underlay to forward packets. A Service Function Forwarder (SFF) reads the encapsulation, sends traffic to attached service functions, and forwards it to the next SFF.

A service function may understand the encapsulation or be unaware of it. An SFC proxy removes the encapsulation before sending traffic to an unaware function and applies it again when the traffic returns. At the domain boundary, ingress adds SFC information and egress removes domain-specific information.
sections.plainLanguage: A classifier assigns traffic to a path. Forwarders use the path information to deliver packets to services, while a proxy supports services that do not read that information themselves.

sections.title: Policy, Metadata, and Operations
sections.content:
Metadata can carry context between classifiers, service functions, and external systems. For example, a classifier may add subscriber information for later service functions. The control plane constructs paths and distributes forwarding information; the architecture leaves its detailed design out of scope.

Solutions must address loops, load balancing, packet-size growth from added headers, operations and maintenance, and resilience to failures. A packet flow should receive consistent handling when service functions or forwarders offer several choices. Limited, policy-compliant loops can exist, but solutions must prevent unbounded loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Metadata can provide context to services as traffic moves along a path. Implementations also need to prevent endless loops, keep packet sizes manageable, and respond to failures.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Changing how traffic moves through a network can change its security and privacy properties. The transport must prevent outsiders from injecting packets that the SFC domain would accept for processing, including through tunnels to other domains.

Metadata may contain sensitive information, including personally identifying information. Realizations MUST protect it and MUST verify that suitable protection is available from where the information is added until it is removed. If that protection is unavailable, the control mechanism SHOULD generate an error notification.
sections.plainLanguage: The network must prevent outsiders from injecting traffic into a service chain. It must also protect sensitive metadata while that information travels through the chain.
